note: What each driver makes of the codes its robot's maker defines, in four classes — DRY-COVERAGE-PLAN.md 12.C.6, the dry proxy for layer 9. ok: healthy (no flag, a zero fault word, commands taken). degraded: running with something wrong (DEGRADED alone, commands taken). fault: the robot is not doing what it is told (FAULT and DEGRADED, commands refused — DEGRADED because §27's rhal condition reads that bit and not FAULT). estop: the maker's stop chain is open (ESTOP and DEGRADED, commands refused). A vocabulary has a kind: an alarm channel's unlisted code escalates (unmapped) to fault or estop, never to ok or degraded; a warning channel — codes the maker documents as advisory — may stop at degraded. probes are codes chosen outside every table, which tools/fault-vocab/contract.py injects and holds the driver to; no_probes says why a vocabulary has none (a bitset or a total decode has no value outside it). fault_code says how the fault word relates to the code: verbatim (the injected code), derived (the subject says how — node << 16 | code for CANopen, a drive's ring position plus one for EtherCAT), or absent (the vocabulary has no code of its own to carry, only the flags). Every code names the maker's own word for it; source says where the table comes from, what was generated from the maker's own source, what was measured against the maker's software and what was only read. not_covered lists a vocabulary or state the driver reads that this table does not cover, with the reason; pending is a driver that is not bound yet and says why; table_of is a Rust port held to its Python twin's table by a test of its own that reads this file. A driver with no entry at all is a check failure (tools/check-fault-vocab.mjs): silence is not an answer. This table is a statement about translation, not about the robot: it says what a driver does with a code, never that the code means what the maker says it means on the machine in front of you.

emcy_error_code.channel: the emergency object a drive sends when something in it changes: COB-ID 0x080 plus the node, the emergency error code in its first two bytes (little-endian)
emcy_error_code.source: CiA 301's emergency error code table, as CANopenNode's `CO_EMC_*` lists it (`301/CO_Emergency.h` at 9b8beed8367241e96ac03f916cd5a500bcb2cf23, Apache-2.0): 35 codes, generated from the header and not retyped, the name each carries being the header's own comment. A table of classes and a few specific codes, not of every code a drive may send: CiA 402's own additions (0x7305, incremental sensor 1 fault, which `slave.py`'s `fault()` sends) and every manufacturer-specific code are not in it, and are the unlisted case. Read, not measured: a drive raises these on events this repository cannot cause.
emcy_error_code.why: an emergency object is an event, not a state: it says something changed in the drive, and the drive may go on running (an over-temperature warning) or may already have faulted (the statusword says which, and is the other vocabulary). Either way the black box wants the code, and the OS wants to know the drive is not well, so a drive with a standing emergency is DEGRADED and the fault word carries the node in its upper half and the code, verbatim, in its lower: `node << 16 | code`. An emergency with the code 0x0000 is CiA 301's error reset, and clears it.

mav_state.channel: HEARTBEAT.system_status (MAV_STATE), read by `read_state` off the latest heartbeat of the one vehicle the driver is bound to
mav_state.source: MAVLink's common dialect, MAV_STATE: nine values. Their names, numbers and the one-line descriptions quoted in `why` are read from pymavlink 2.4.49's generated common dialect (`pymavlink/dialects/v20/common.py`), and `make check-layout` holds the driver's names and numbers to it when it is run, which CI does not do per push. The classes are this table's reading and are not measured: that ArduPilot reports CRITICAL or EMERGENCY while one of its failsafes is flying the vehicle is read, not seen, and no firmware was made to report CRITICAL, EMERGENCY, POWEROFF or FLIGHT_TERMINATION (the SITL suite never provokes them).
mav_state.why: MAV_STATE is the autopilot's own account of what it is doing, and the one thing in a heartbeat that says a failsafe has fired. The first three values are 'not up yet' (degraded: the vehicle itself refuses to arm and says so, and the motions are taken as far as it allows); STANDBY and ACTIVE are the two healthy ones; CRITICAL, EMERGENCY and POWEROFF say the vehicle is flying its own failsafe, is losing the airframe or is shutting down (fault); FLIGHT_TERMINATION is the autopilot ending the flight, which is as final a stop as the maker has (estop).

0.name: MAV_STATE_UNINIT
0.why: the dialect says 'state is unknown': a vehicle that has not said what it is doing is not known to be well, and is not stopped either

1.name: MAV_STATE_BOOT
1.why: the dialect says the system is booting up: not flight-ready, and the vehicle refuses what it cannot do in its own words

2.name: MAV_STATE_CALIBRATING
2.why: the dialect says the system is calibrating and not flight-ready

5.name: MAV_STATE_CRITICAL
5.why: the dialect says a non-normal flight mode in which the system can however still navigate; ArduPilot's failsafes are what put it there, so this reads it as a failsafe the vehicle is flying itself. It is not doing what this driver last asked, and a new motion would fight the failsafe; the way out (`hold`, `rtl`, `land`, `disarm`) stays open

6.name: MAV_STATE_EMERGENCY
6.why: the dialect says a non-normal flight mode in which the system lost control over parts or the whole airframe, in mayday and going down: nothing it is asked to do can be relied on, and `land` and `disarm` are what a person has left

7.name: MAV_STATE_POWEROFF
7.why: the dialect says the power-down sequence has begun and the system will shut down now: there is no better class for a body about to be gone, and a motion it will not hear is not accepted

8.name: MAV_STATE_FLIGHT_TERMINATION
8.why: the dialect says the system is terminating itself: the autopilot ending the flight, motors cut, a parachute or a fall. Read as the maker's stop chain, closed for good, and nothing moves the body

mav_state.unmapped_because: MAV_STATE is one byte and the dialect defines nine of its values: a vehicle that reports another is firmware this table was not written for, and the state of an autopilot nobody has described is not read as healthy
mav_state.keeps_because: a vehicle in a failsafe is moved by what the person asks of it and not by joint commands: `hold` and `rtl` and `land` are how a vehicle is brought down or to rest, and `disarm` (with force=1 in the air, the driver's own rule) is the last thing a person has when the airframe is lost. A driver that refuses them because the heartbeat says CRITICAL has taken the way out away at the moment it matters; a flight termination refuses them with the rest, because there is nothing left for them to move

system_fault_severity.channel: `SystemFault.severity` of every fault in `system_fault_state.faults` (the faults that are active now; `historical_faults`, which the maker says have cleared, are not read), in `GetRobotState`
system_fault_severity.source: Boston Dynamics' own `robot_state.proto` (boston-dynamics/spot-sdk, master, fetched 2026-10-01, sha256 678766f6928b568c…): the enumeration's names and numbers are generated from `bosdyn-api` 5.2.0's compiled descriptors, which the driver's own client imports, and the one-line descriptions quoted in `why` are the proto's comments. Nothing here was measured against the maker's robot. Boston Dynamics ships no simulator of the gRPC API, and the fake in this tree reports whatever the suite tells it to, so the table's classes are read from the maker's descriptions and never seen on a robot.
system_fault_severity.why: the maker says an active system fault is an indicator of a hardware or software problem that 'may indicate the robot may fail to comply with a user request' — a failure to enable motor power, a loss of perception, a fault recovery behaviour — and gives the severity as the indication of how bad. Read as three classes: INFO is no problem (ok), WARN is a robot that may perform worse (degraded), and CRITICAL, or a severity the maker has not graded, is a robot that cannot be relied on to do what it is told (fault). In `fault` the driver refuses the motions that take the body somewhere new (`power_on`, `stand`, `selfright`) and still answers `stop`, `sit` and `power_off`. When several faults are active the worst class wins and the fault word is that fault's own `code` — Boston Dynamics' number for the variety of fault, 'useful for Boston Dynamics support staff to diagnose' it — so the black box carries what a person can look up.

0.why: the maker's 'Unknown severity': a fault the robot did not grade is read as one that could be critical, and not as harmless

1.name: SEVERITY_INFO
1.why: the maker's own description is 'No hardware problem': the OS is not told the robot is impaired because it has something to say

2.name: SEVERITY_WARN
2.why: the maker's own description is 'Robot performance may be degraded': running, with something wrong, which is DEGRADED and nothing worse

3.name: SEVERITY_CRITICAL
3.why: the maker's 'Critical fault'; of a battery fault at this severity the maker's field comment says the robot is 'likely' going to shut down immediately

With a critical fault `stop` holds the robot where it is, `sit` brings it to the ground and `power_off` cuts the motors: the three things a person has when a fault says the robot may shut down, and a driver that refuses them because the state says critical has taken the way out away at the moment it matters

The first two are DEGRADED and commands are accepted; a major fault is FAULT with DEGRADED, and a command the gripper is not taking is refused, because answering it OK would be success the driver did not have.

gripper_enable.source: AgileX's own SDK, `agilexrobotics/piper_sdk` at c9e8a281 (2026-07-31, the pin `drivers/piper/layout_check.py` holds), names generated from its enumerations and flag classes and not retyped: ArmMsgFeedBackGripper.FOC_Status.driver_enable_status. gripper_enable.why: a hand that has disabled itself is not taking commands; the driver faults, as for a joint driver, with the same 0x40 in the top byte.
gripper_enable.unmapped_because: a bit has two values and both are listed.
gripper_enable.no_probes: a single bit has no value outside its table
gripper_enable.fault_code_is: 0x40 in the top byte for a disabled gripper, and zero for an enabled one

ctrl_mode.channel: the control mode byte of every status frame (0x2A1 byte 0), read every cycle
ctrl_mode.source: AgileX's own SDK, `agilexrobotics/piper_sdk` at c9e8a281 (2026-07-31, the pin `drivers/piper/layout_check.py` holds), names generated from its enumerations and flag classes and not retyped: ArmMsgFeedbackStatusEnum.CtrlMode, eight values. ctrl_mode.why: CAN control is the one mode in which the arm takes this master's joint targets. ctrl_mode.unmapped_because: the mode is a value the driver compares with CAN control: a value the table does not define is not CAN control.
ctrl_mode.fault_code_is: bit 15 of the fault word (FAULT_NOT_CAN_CONTROL) for any mode but CAN control, and zero for CAN control

not_covered.what: the drivers' voltage, temperature and current numbers (0x251 to 0x266)
not_covered.why: the driver reads each driver's status byte and never the analogue values: the maker's own thresholds raise the over-temperature, over-current and low-voltage flags, so a number the driver compared with a limit of its own would be a second, unsourced threshold beside the maker's.

not_covered.what: the move mode, teach status, motion status and trajectory number of the status frame
not_covered.why: none is a fault: the move mode is what this driver set, motion status says whether a target was reached (the positions say the same), and the teach and trajectory fields belong to modes this driver does not speak. A teaching state is in `arm_status` and in `ctrl_mode`.

not_covered.what: the gripper's zeroing bit (0x2A8 byte 6, bit 7)
not_covered.why: a gripper that has not been zeroed reports a stroke from an arbitrary origin, which is a calibration state and not a fault; `homing` is reported as unreported for the whole body (the arm's joints report no zeroing state at all), and the zeroing command is never sent.

fault.channel: the fault register (0x00f) while the mode register (0x000) reads 1, fault; both are in the query every cycle
fault.source: mjbots's own firmware, `mjbots/moteus` at 8f747f4a (2026-09-27, the pin `drivers/moteus/layout_check.py` holds): `fw/error.h`, `errc` 32 to 50, generated and not retyped, with `docs/protocol/registers.md`'s table of the same codes held name for name by the layout check. Read, not measured: the maker's firmware raises these on events this repository cannot cause, and mjbots publishes no simulator of the controller.
fault.why: mode 1 is a controller that has taken its output stage off and ignores every command but a stop (`ISR_MaybeChangeMode`: from fault a command returns). The driver faults, refuses commands whole, and never writes the stop that clears it: the clear is a person's act at the controller, and `open` is the only place an axis is brought up. The code is carried in the fault word, with the joint and the mode beside it.
fault.unmapped_because: in mode 1 the register holds a code from a firmware that may be newer than this table, and every state in which a controller has faulted is a fault whatever its number: reading an unknown one as healthy would clear a fault nobody read. The probes are values the table does not define, including the firmware's own transport codes (1 to 7), which are not servo states and which a faulted controller could only carry by mistake.
fault.fault_code_is: joint number (from 1) in bits 16 and up, the mode (1) in bits 8 to 15, and the injected code in the low byte

limiting.channel: the fault register (0x00f) while the mode register reads 10, position; both are in the query every cycle
limiting.source: mjbots's own firmware, `mjbots/moteus` at 8f747f4a (2026-09-27, the pin `drivers/moteus/layout_check.py` holds): `fw/error.h`, `errc` 96 to 105. The register reference (`registers.md`) lists 96 to 103; the firmware defines 104 (flux braking) and 105 (field weakening) as well, which it does not (F285), and the table is the firmware's because it is the firmware that sends them. Read, not measured: the maker's firmware raises these on events this repository cannot cause, and mjbots publishes no simulator of the controller.
limiting.why: in a valid control mode a non-zero code says which function is limiting the output (`registers.md`: *not faults*). The controller keeps running and takes commands, so the driver reads DEGRADED alone and carries the code in the fault word, joint and mode beside it, so the black box says which function; an unlisted non-zero code is never read as healthy.
limiting.unmapped_because: a warning channel's floor is `degraded`: a code the table does not list is a limit from a firmware newer than this table, which the controller runs on through, and which is not read as healthy and not as a stop.
limiting.fault_code_is: joint number (from 1) in bits 16 and up, the mode (10) in bits 8 to 15, and the injected code in the low byte

mode.channel: the mode register (0x000), read every cycle for each controller
mode.source: mjbots's own firmware, `mjbots/moteus` at 8f747f4a (2026-09-27, the pin `drivers/moteus/layout_check.py` holds): `fw/bldc_servo_structs.h`, `BldcServoMode`, sixteen values, generated and not retyped, with the maker's Python client's `Mode` held against it by the layout check. Read, not measured: the maker's firmware raises these on events this repository cannot cause, and mjbots publishes no simulator of the controller.
mode.why: position is the one mode this driver put an axis in and the one in which it takes commands. Any other mode in a session is something done to the axis by someone else or by the controller itself — stopped, a preparing phase, another master's pwm, voltage, current, stay-within or measure-inductance, a watchdog timeout, or a zero-velocity or brake stop this driver did not write — and the driver faults, refuses commands whole, and sends nothing to bring the axis back: a driver that re-enabled an axis a person had stopped would be starting a machine whose reason for stopping nobody had looked at. The stop it writes itself is read against its own latch (the suite's, `emergency_stop`).
mode.unmapped_because: the mode is a value the driver compares with position: a value the table does not define is not position. The probes are values the register can carry as an int8 above the firmware's last mode.
mode.fault_code_is: joint number (from 1) in bits 16 and up and the mode in bits 8 to 15, with the fault register in the low byte (zero outside mode 1)

not_covered.what: the firmware's codes 1 to 7 (DMA stream and UART errors)
not_covered.why: they are the diagnostic port's transport errors, raised on the controller's serial interface and not states of the servo; no register this driver reads carries them, and the contract's probes include some of them to show a faulted controller holding one is read as a fault.

not_covered.what: the motor driver's own fault registers (0x140 and 0x141)
not_covered.why: they carry the gate driver's bit fields only when the fault code is 33 (motor driver fault), which this driver already reads as a fault with the code in its word; the bits say *why* the gate driver faulted (under-voltage, over-current, over-temperature), which a person reads from the controller, and this driver would have no different thing to do with any of them.

not_covered.what: the driver's own stop (modes 0, 12 and 15 after `emergency_stop`)
not_covered.why: the contract's `estop` class is the maker's stop chain being open, and a moteus has no such signal on the wire: the stop here is the driver's own latch and the mode the operator named. That is held by the suite (the latch against an arm that is deaf to the stop, the mode written, the release that is honest only where the driver stays on), not by a code a maker defined.

not_covered.what: the home state (0x00c), the voltage and the temperature
not_covered.why: none is a fault. The home state is reported as the homing bits of the state word (output-referenced reads as homed, anything else as pending) and held by the suite; the voltage and the temperature are read and not compared with any limit of this driver's own, because the controller's own thresholds raise fault codes 34, 38 and 40 and a number this driver compared with a limit it chose would be a second, unsourced threshold beside the maker's.

error_byte.channel: ERROR(m), six bytes at 1606 to 1611, one per actuator, read every cycle (with STATUS, in one twelve-byte read)
error_byte.source: Inspire Robots' own manuals: the RH56 series user manual PRJ-02-TS-U-001 V1.0.9 §2.4.18 (sha256 f16c9247a481) and the RH56DFTP user manual PRJ-02-TS-U-010 V1.0.0 §2.6.18 (sha256 4cad22265b48): the five bits, generated from the text of both (the two tables are identical) and not retyped. Read, not measured: no hand was reached, and the maker's simulator does not exist.
error_byte.why: an error bit is an actuator that has stopped for cause. Four of the five (locked rotor, over-current, abnormal operation of the motor, a communication error) clear when written to CLEAR_ERROR, which is the `clear_errors` motion and never the driver's own; over-temperature is "not clearable" and clears when the actuator cools. The manual does not say what a hand does with a command while an error is held, so none is sent: a hand holding any error bit is FAULT with DEGRADED and a command is refused, because answering one OK would be success the driver did not have.

8.name: 0x08 bit 3: Abnormal operation of the motor

error_byte.unmapped_because: the byte is a bitset the driver reads whole: a bit the table does not define (5, 6, 7) is an error from a firmware newer than this table, and masking it to healthy would clear a fault nobody read. The probes are the three undefined single bits and two combinations of them with a defined one.
error_byte.fault_code_is: joint number (from 1) in bits 16 and up, the status byte in bits 8 to 15 and the error byte in the low byte, of the lowest-numbered joint that holds a fault

status_byte.channel: STATUS(m), six bytes at 1612 to 1617, one per actuator, read every cycle (with ERROR)
status_byte.source: the RH56 series user manual PRJ-02-TS-U-001 V1.0.9 §2.4.19 (sha256 f16c9247a481): the seven codes, generated from its text. **The RH56DFTP manual lists the STATUS register and gives no table of its codes**, so on a DFTP the meaning of a status code rests on the series manual's. Read, not measured.
status_byte.why: status 0 to 3 are a finger doing its job (unclenching, grasping, stopped at the target, stopped at the force limit) and say nothing is wrong. 5, 6 and 7 are the maker's own words for a stop for cause (current protection, locked rotor, actuator fault): FAULT with DEGRADED, and a command is refused. Code 4 and everything above 7 are in no table.

3.name: 3 Stop after reaching the defined force control value

6.name: 6 Stop due to locked-rotor of the actuator

status_byte.unmapped_because: a driver that cannot tell what a finger is doing does not command it: a code the table does not list is a state from a firmware newer than this table, and reading it as healthy would be a guess about the one thing the manual leaves open. The probes are the hole at 4 and values above 7.
status_byte.fault_code_is: joint number (from 1) in bits 16 and up, the status byte in bits 8 to 15 and the error byte in the low byte, of the lowest-numbered joint that holds a fault

not_covered.what: CURRENT (1594), FORCE_ACT (1582) and TEMP (1618)
not_covered.why: none is a fault. The current protection, the locked rotor and the over-temperature are the hand's own, and each raises its own error bit and status, which are covered; this driver reads the three on demand (the `status` motion) and compares none with a limit of its own, because a threshold this driver chose would be a second, unsourced one beside the maker's.

not_covered.what: the Modbus and CAN faults of the DFTP and the CAN supplement's own
not_covered.why: this driver speaks the RS-485 private protocol and refuses Modbus by name (the byte registers' order under Modbus is not in the manuals); a CAN transport is not built, so no error frame of either is read.

not_covered.what: the hand's own emergency stop
not_covered.why: the manuals document none: the `estop` class is a maker's stop chain being open, and an Inspire hand has no such signal on the wire. The stop here is the driver's own latch and the hold it writes, which the suite holds.

rg_safety_bits.channel: the RG2 and RG6 status word (register 268, the eleventh of the state block at 258), bits 2 to 6: safety switch 1 pushed and triggered, safety switch 2 pushed and triggered, and the safety DC error; read every cycle
rg_safety_bits.source: the maker's own client library, `libonrobot_tool_api` 1.2.0 (BSD-3-Clause): `RgDiagnostics` in `diagnostics.hpp` names the five bits (`safety_1_pushed`, `safety_1_triggered`, `safety_2_pushed`, `safety_2_triggered`, `safety_dc_error`) and the bit positions were read off the library by running it (`layout_check.py` repeats the experiments). The library says nothing about what any of them means for the machine, and neither does anything else this repository could read.
rg_safety_bits.why: a pushed or triggered safety switch and a safety DC error are the gripper's own safety circuit speaking, and what the gripper does with a command while one is set is not documented, so none is sent: a gripper reporting any of them is FAULT with DEGRADED and a command is refused, because answering one OK would be success the driver did not have. They are `fault` and not `estop` because the library does not say the stop chain is open: an RG's switches are inputs the integrator wires, and which one means 'stop' is theirs. The DC error is the one the driver's own message says software cannot clear (a power cycle after the equipment is made safe).
rg_safety_bits.unmapped_because: the field is five named bits read whole and every combination of them is a state of the safety circuit: a combination the table does not list is still made of bits it does, so the driver's rule (any set bit is a fault) covers it. Bits 10 to 15 of the status word are named by nothing and are not read (see not_covered).
rg_safety_bits.no_probes: a bitset the driver reads whole: every single bit it reads is in the table, and the bits above them belong to the error code (the next vocabulary) or to nothing the maker names
rg_safety_bits.fault_code_is: the status word masked to bits 2 to 9, as the maker lays it out: the safety bits in bits 2 to 6 and the error code in bits 7 to 9

rg_error_code.channel: the RG2 and RG6 status word, bits 7 to 9: a three-bit error code
rg_error_code.source: the maker's own client library, `libonrobot_tool_api` 1.2.0: `RgDiagnostics::error_code` (`uint8_t`) in `diagnostics.hpp`, and the field's position read off the library by running it. **The library publishes no table of what any value means**, and nor does anything else this repository could read, so no value has a name here. Read off the library, not measured on a gripper.
rg_error_code.why: a nonzero error code is the gripper saying something is wrong without saying what. Zero is the only value that says nothing is wrong, so every other value is FAULT with DEGRADED and a command is refused: the driver reports the code as the maker gives it, in the fault word and in its message, and does not interpret one.

hardware_error_status.channel: Hardware_Error_Status (address 70, one byte) of each of the hand's sixteen servos, read every cycle (with Torque_Enable, in one synchronised read of 64 to 70)
hardware_error_status.source: ROBOTIS's e-manual for the XC330-M288-T and the XL330-M288-T (https://emanual.robotis.com/docs/en/dxl/x/xc330-m288/, Hardware Error Status): bit 0 input voltage error, bit 2 overheating error, bit 4 electrical shock error, bit 5 overload error; bits 1, 3, 6 and 7 are not named. Read, not measured: no servo was reached.
hardware_error_status.why: a hardware error is a servo that has stopped for cause. With the factory Shutdown setting (52: overload, electrical shock, overheating) the servo has switched its torque off, and a servo holding such an error takes no torque back until it is rebooted. The e-manual says nothing about what an input voltage error does, and nothing about how a servo answers a goal while one is held, so none is sent: a hand holding any bit is FAULT with DEGRADED and a command is refused, because answering one OK would be success the driver did not have. Clearing is a reboot (the `clear_errors` motion with `confirm=limp`), which drops the servo's torque and its gains, so it is a person's and never the driver's own.

alarm_id.source: Dobot's own Python client for the V4 controllers (https://github.com/Dobot-Arm/TCP-IP-Python-V4, MIT), `demo/files/alarmController.py`: 341 controller alarms with an identifier, a level (0, 1 or 5) and a description in ten languages, of which the English is used here. The table was generated from that file, not typed; the client was run against this repository's simulated controller (`layout_check.py`), no Dobot controller was. The classes are this driver's reading of the descriptions and not the maker's: the table gives a level but the interface document does not say what a level means, so none is read from it.
alarm_id.why: an alarm is the controller refusing to move. The interface document says that in RobotMode 9 the arm takes no motion command, so every alarm is `fault` (FAULT and DEGRADED, commands refused). Three are the maker's own words for a stop: 116 "The emergency stop button is captured", 132 "The software emergency stop signal is triggered" and 133 "The user emergency stop signal is triggered", and those are `estop`. Others mention a stop or the safety system (1430 "Power off after emergency stop", 2050 "Protective stop timeout alarm", 2132 "Emergency stop line detection exception alarm") and are the aftermath or a fault in the stop line, not the stop being pressed, so they stay `fault`. Clearing an alarm is the `clear_errors` motion, and an emergency stop is released first (`EmergencyStop(0)`): a person's, never the driver's own.

alarm_id.unmapped_because: an alarm identifier that is in no table is an alarm from a controller newer than this one, or a servo's (the maker's client carries a second table, `alarmServo.py`, whose identifiers are not read here): a controller that lists an alarm refuses motion, so it is read as the arm not doing what it is told, and never as healthy.

robot_mode.channel: RobotMode in the feedback packet (offset 24, an 8-byte integer), read in every packet
robot_mode.source: Dobot's TCP/IP remote control interface document V4.6.6, `RobotMode()` (values 1 to 11), the same numbers as the feedback's RobotMode field; the names are the maker's own client's (`ROBOT_MODE_*`), except 11, which the document calls a collision and the client calls a jog. Read, and run against this repository's simulated controller; no Dobot controller was reached.
robot_mode.why: the modes in which the arm takes a motion command are enabled and idle (5), running (7) and a single move (8): `ok`. An alarm (9) and a collision (11) are `fault`. The fault word of 9 is the first alarm of the list when it has been read and 9 itself when it has not (the maker's alarm table starts at 16, so 9 is never an alarm), and of 11 it is 11. Any value the document does not list (0, 12 and up) is a state of the arm nobody here has read about, so it is `fault`, and its word is 65536 plus the mode, above every alarm identifier of the maker's table.

9.name: ROBOT_MODE_ERROR: alarm
9.why: the controller is in its alarm state and takes no command; the alarm list (`GetErrorID()`) says which

11.name: ROBOT_MODE_COLLISION: collision detected
11.why: the controller has detected a collision and stopped the arm; the interface document gives the value as a collision, where the maker's own client names it a jog

robot_mode.unmapped_because: a RobotMode the document does not list is a state of the arm that this table has no word for; it is not read as healthy.
robot_mode.fault_code_is: 9 for an alarm with no alarm list read, 11 for a collision, and 65536 plus the mode for a mode the document does not list

not_covered.what: RobotMode 1 (initialising), 2 (a brake is open), 3 (powered off), 4 (disabled), 6 (drag) and 10 (paused)
not_covered.why: in each the arm takes no motion command and none is a fault: the driver reports DEGRADED and refuses the command (EPERM, naming the motion that changes the state: `power_on`, `enable`). The contract has no class for that: its `degraded` takes commands and its `fault` sets FAULT. `selftest.py` holds each of the six.

not_covered.what: the packet's `SafetyState` byte (offset 1420) and `DragStatus`
not_covered.why: the interface document gives the byte no bit table in anything read here, so a reading of its bits would be this driver's own invention. A stop is read from the alarm list, where the maker names it. The byte is decoded and not used.

not_covered.what: the servo alarm table (`alarmServo.py`) and an alarm on a joint's drive
not_covered.why: the interface document does not say whether `GetErrorID()` lists servo identifiers beside the controller's, or in what range; the driver reads whatever the list holds, and an identifier it does not know is `fault` (the probes). Which servo raised it is not said.

not_covered.what: the controller's own emergency stop wiring
not_covered.why: the controller's stop is a hardware chain, and this driver sees it only as alarm 116 or 133 after the fact. The driver's own stop is a software one (`Stop()` or `EmergencyStop(1)`) and says so: it is not the chain.

error_code.channel: the controller's `error[code][N]` line on the command port (5000): the controller says an error once, the bridge holds each code it reads until the `clear_faults` motion acknowledges it (refused while the packet still shows a cause), and the fault word is the first held code, a stop's before any other
error_code.source: Rainbow Robotics' own client `rbpodo` (Apache-2.0, https://github.com/RainbowRobotics/rbpodo, commit f6ef41ad), `include/rbpodo/error_code.hpp`: `ErrorCodeMessage`, 606 codes (0 to 605), each with a Korean and an English text, of which the English is used here. The table was generated from that file (`sim/gen_codes.py`), not typed, and `layout_check.py` runs the maker's client against this repository's simulated controller. Read, and run against that simulator; no Rainbow arm and no Rainbow control box was reached. The classes are this driver's reading of the texts and not the maker's: the table says neither which of its codes arrive as an `error` and which as a `warn` or an `info`, nor what the controller does with a command while one is held.
error_code.why: an `error` line is the controller reporting something it did not do or cannot do, and the one table it uses for `info`, `warn` and `error` does not say which code goes on which channel, so every code that arrives as an `error` is read as the arm not doing what it is told: `fault` (FAULT and DEGRADED, commands refused, because an answer of OK to a command the controller is ignoring is success the driver did not have). Eleven are about the stop chain in the maker's own words (60, 253, 254, 255, 256, 257, 258, 485, 486, 487, 488: the Safety switches 'open or closed', the EMS 1 and 2, PRS, HSS and SSS switches, 'powered off by the ... Safety switch', and 60 'Control Box GP Switch Error Check Protective stop connector') and are `estop`. Codes whose text is about the safety parameters, walls and polygons (222 to 240, 496, 497, 520, 521) or an 'emergency direct teach' (259, 297, 490) are not the stop chain, and on the `error` channel they stay `fault`. Acknowledging is the `clear_faults` motion, which is a person's to ask for; a stop chain is closed at the control box.

error_code.unmapped_because: an `error` line whose code is in no table is an error from a controller newer than this table: it is still the controller saying it did not do something, so the arm is read as not doing what it is told, and never as healthy.

warn_code.channel: the controller's `warn[code][N]` line on the command port (5000): the controller says a warning once, after it has acknowledged the command it is about; the bridge shows DEGRADED for two seconds with the code as the fault word, and refuses the next command once (EINVAL, naming the warning) so that the person sending commands hears it
warn_code.source: Rainbow Robotics' own client `rbpodo` (Apache-2.0, https://github.com/RainbowRobotics/rbpodo, commit f6ef41ad), `include/rbpodo/error_code.hpp`: `ErrorCodeMessage`, 606 codes (0 to 605), each with a Korean and an English text, of which the English is used here. The table was generated from that file (`sim/gen_codes.py`), not typed, and `layout_check.py` runs the maker's client against this repository's simulated controller. Read, and run against that simulator; no Rainbow arm and no Rainbow control box was reached. The classes are this driver's reading of the texts and not the maker's: the table says neither which of its codes arrive as an `error` and which as a `warn` or an `info`, nor what the controller does with a command while one is held.
warn_code.why: a `warn` line is the controller's advisory channel: it carries on, so the arm is `degraded` (DEGRADED alone, commands taken) and never a fault. The table is the one the `error` channel uses and does not say which of its codes arrive as warnings, so none is singled out, and one that is about the stop chain is no stop when it comes as a warning. The bridge tells the person at the next command by refusing it once, as the controller's answer to the command before it; the contract's command is sent again in that case (the subject says so), and a refusal that goes on would fail it.

sos_flag.channel: `op_stat_sos_flag` in the state packet (offset 448, an integer, the low six bits valid), read in every packet
sos_flag.source: Rainbow Robotics' own packet document, `reqdata_Structure` 6.10 (the state packet a `reqdata` returns on the data port, 580 bytes), which `layout_check.py` holds the driver's offsets to by running the maker's client on the same bytes. Read, and run against this repository's simulated controller; no Rainbow arm and no Rainbow control box was reached.
sos_flag.why: the document calls it the 'robot arm device error code during operation' and lists twelve; it does not say what the arm does with a command while one is set, so none is sent: a nonzero flag is `fault` (FAULT and DEGRADED, commands refused). None of the twelve is the stop chain in its words, so none is `estop`. The fault word is the flag in a band of its own above every code of the maker's message table.
sos_flag.unmapped_because: a device error number the document does not list (13 to 63) is a device error from a controller newer than this document, and a flag of any value is a device saying something is wrong: it is not read as healthy. The document says only the low six bits are valid, so a value from 64 up is read as its low six bits and is not probed.

ems_flag.why: the document calls it the 'software (kinematics) emergency stop situation' and lists four: arm stretch, Cartesian limit, joint limit, un-solvable. The words are about a pose the controller's own software would not take, not about the stop chain, so a nonzero flag is `fault` (commands refused) and not `estop`. The fault word is the flag in a band of its own.

collision.why: the document says 'whether out-collision is detected (0 or 1)'. A detected collision has stopped the arm's program (code 3 of the maker's table is 'Program is Stopped because of Collision-Detection'), so it is `fault`; the `resume` motion with `after=collision` is how a person goes on. The fault word is the value in a band of its own.

joint_info.channel: `jnt_info[6]` in the state packet (offset 372, six integers, one a joint), read in every packet. The code here is the joint (0 for the base to 5 for the third wrist) times 256 plus the bit, the one error bit set in that joint's word
joint_info.source: Rainbow Robotics' own packet document, `reqdata_Structure` 6.10 (the state packet a `reqdata` returns on the data port, 580 bytes), which `layout_check.py` holds the driver's offsets to by running the maker's client on the same bytes. Read, and run against this repository's simulated controller; no Rainbow arm and no Rainbow control box was reached.
joint_info.why: each of bits 4 to 15 of a joint's word is, in the document's words, an encoder error (Nonius, low battery, calibration mode, multi-turn) or a joint error state (JAM, CUR, BIG, INP, FLT, TMP, PS1, PS2), and a joint that reports one is not doing what it is told: `fault` (commands refused). The fault word is the joint and the bit in a band of its own, so that the black box says which joint and which error.

0.name: no error bit in any joint's word (bits 0 to 3, the FET, RUN, INIT and MODE state, are not errors)

joint_info.unmapped_because: every bit of the word that the document names is in the table, and an unlisted one is not a code but a reserved bit.
joint_info.no_probes: the word is a bitset of which every bit from 0 to 15 is named (0 to 3 are state, 4 to 15 errors) and bits 16 to 31 are 'reserved' by the document: there is no code outside the table to probe. The reserved bits are in `not_covered`.
joint_info.fault_code_is: 262144 plus the joint times 256 plus the bit

mode.source: Rainbow Robotics' own packet document, `reqdata_Structure` 6.10 (the state packet a `reqdata` returns on the data port, 580 bytes), which `layout_check.py` holds the driver's offsets to by running the maker's client on the same bytes. Read, and run against this repository's simulated controller; no Rainbow arm and no Rainbow control box was reached.
mode.why: the document lists 0 for a real robot and 1 for the simulation. The subject opens the bridge with `simulator: true`, so the simulation is the mode that takes commands (`ok`); the other listed mode is not a state of the arm but a disagreement between the controller and what the operator said, and is in `not_covered`. A value the document does not list (2 to 15) is a state nobody here has read about: `fault`, with the value in a band of its own above every code of the maker's table.

1.name: 1 = Simulation mode (the mode `simulator: true` asks for)

mode.unmapped_because: a mode the document does not list is a state of the controller that this table has no word for; it is not read as healthy.

not_covered.what: a controller in the mode the operator did not ask for (mode 0 under `simulator: true`, mode 1 under `simulator: false`), an arm that is not activated (`init_state_info` below 6, in the real mode), and one that is paused (the task state or `op_stat_soft_estop_occur`)
not_covered.why: in each the arm takes no motion command and none is a fault: the driver reports DEGRADED and refuses the command (EPERM, naming the motion that changes the state: `set_mode`, `activate`, `resume`). The contract has no class for that: its `degraded` takes commands and its `fault` sets FAULT. `selftest.py` holds each of them.

not_covered.what: bits 16 to 31 of a joint's `jnt_info` word, 'reserved' in the document
not_covered.why: the document gives them no meaning, so reading one as an error would be this driver's invention, and the driver does not read them. A reserved bit that a later controller gives a meaning is a change the probes of this table cannot reach.

not_covered.what: the control box's E-Stop states 1 and 2 (`information_chunk_1` bits 3 and 5) and `op_stat_self_collision`
not_covered.why: the document says which bit is which switch and not which value is a pressed stop, and gives the self-collision field a bit table whose meaning of 'last out-collision state' is not said: reading either would be this driver's own invention. A stop is read from the error codes, where the maker names it (253 to 258, 485 to 488, 60). `status` reports the two bits as sent.

not_covered.what: the controller's own emergency stop wiring
not_covered.why: the controller's stop is a hardware chain, and this driver sees it only as an error code or a changed field after the fact. The driver's own stop is `task stop` with a latch of its own, and says so: it is not the chain, and the controller was seen to leave its stop unlatched.

tello.pending: nothing to cover: the SDK 2.0 User Guide publishes no table of error codes. A reply is `ok`, `error` or free text, the state string carries no fault field, and the driver's fault word stays 0 with its own stop latch as the only flag. A table cannot be generated from a vocabulary that is not published, and a threshold on the battery or the temperature would be this driver inventing a vendor fault (the battery floor is the operator's, `low_battery_percent`, and degrades). Revisit if Ryze or DJI publish one
